In this study, we identified a novel transcription state, termed ‘transcription resistive’, which shares active histone markers with transcriptionally active genes but displays the undetectable transcription activities of silencing genes (marked by H3K27me3 and H3K9me2).
We termed this chromatin state ‘transcriptional resistive’, which is distinctive from traditional transcription activation and transcription silencing.

Furthermore, we performed NET-seq using rice seedlings and the results showed much less transcription activity of Pol II on these H3K36me3-elevated genes (Extended Data Fig. 6c,f). By reanalyzing published FAIRE-seq data27, interestingly, we observed that these H3K36me3-elevated genes showed more open-chromatin states compared with H3K9me2-marked genes (Extended Data Fig. 6d,f), exhibiting a chromatin transcription-resistive state similar to those of C3 genes in Arabidopsis.
Our data reveal a previously undiscovered function of H3K36me3 and transcription regulation.

Furthermore, we unexpectedly found that a large proportion of the coding genome exists as a chromatin state that is open chromatin, marked by H3K36me3, occupied by RNA polymerase II, and looked similar to the ready-for-transcription state but with little to no transcription activity (similar to the level of silencing), even with heat stimulation.
